Programming living cells

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A programming language has been developed that can be used by anyone to program living cells

Unique Selling Point:
Amazing medical breakthrough

Summary:
MIT biological engineers have created a programming language that allows them to rapidly design complex, DNA-encoded circuits that give new functions to living cells. Using this language, anyone can write a program for the function they want, such as detecting and responding to certain environmental conditions. They can then generate a DNA sequence that will achieve it.


Further information:
MIT biological engineers have created a programming language that allows them to rapidly design complex, DNA-encoded circuits that give new functions to living cells.
Using this language, anyone can write a program for the function they want, such as detecting and responding to certain environmental conditions. They can then generate a DNA sequence that will achieve it.

“It is literally a programming language for bacteria,” says Christopher Voigt, an MIT professor of biological engineering. “You use a text-based language, just like you’re programming a computer. Then you take that text and you compile it and it turns it into a DNA sequence that you put into the cell, and the circuit runs inside the cell.”

Voigt and colleagues at Boston University and the National Institute of Standards and Technology have used this language, which they describe in the April 1 issue of Science, to build circuits that can detect up to three inputs and respond in different ways.

Future applications for this kind of programming include designing bacterial cells that can produce a cancer drug when they detect a tumor, or creating yeast cells that can halt their own fermentation process if too many toxic by-products build up.

The researchers plan to make the user design interface available on the Web.
No experience needed.

Over the past 15 years, biologists and engineers have designed many genetic parts, such as sensors, memory switches, and biological clocks that can be combined to modify existing cell functions and add new ones.

However, designing each circuit is a laborious process that requires great expertise and often a lot of trial and error. “You have to have this really intimate knowledge of how those pieces are going to work and how they’re going to come together,” Voigt says.

Users of the new programming language, however, need no special knowledge of genetic engineering.

“You could be completely naive as to how any of it works. That’s what’s really different about this,” Voigt says. “You could be a student in high school and go onto the Web-based server and type out the program you want, and it spits back the DNA sequence.”

The language is based on Verilog, which is commonly used to program computer chips. To create a version of the language that would work for cells, the researchers designed computing elements such as logic gates and sensors that can be encoded in a bacterial cell’s DNA.

The sensors can detect different compounds, such as oxygen or glucose, as well as light, temperature, acidity, and other environmental conditions. Users can also add their own sensors. “It’s very customizable,” Voigt says.

The biggest challenge, he says, was designing the 14 logic gates used in the circuits so that they wouldn’t interfere with each other once placed in the complex environment of a living cell.

In the current version of the programming language, these genetic parts are optimized for E. coli, but the researchers are working on expanding the language for other strains of bacteria, including Bacteroides, commonly found in the human gut, and Pseudomonas, which often lives in plant roots, as well as the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. This would allow users to write a single program and then compile it for different organisms to get the right DNA sequence for each one.

Biological circuits
Using this language, the researchers programmed 60 circuits with different functions, and 45 of them worked correctly the first time they were tested. Many of the circuits were designed to measure one or more environmental conditions, such as oxygen level or glucose concentration, and respond accordingly. Another circuit was designed to rank three different inputs and then respond based on the priority of each one.

One of the new circuits is the largest biological circuit ever built, containing seven logic gates and about 12,000 base pairs of DNA.

Another advantage of this technique is its speed. Until now, “it would take years to build these types of circuits. Now you just hit the button and immediately get a DNA sequence to test,” Voigt says.

His team plans to work on several different applications using this approach: bacteria that can be swallowed to aid in digestion of lactose; bacteria that can live on plant roots and produce insecticide if they sense the plant is under attack; and yeast that can be engineered to shut off when they are producing too many toxic byproducts in a fermentation reactor.

The lead author of the Science paper is MIT graduate student Alec Nielsen. Other authors are former MIT postdoc Bryan Der, MIT postdoc Jonghyeon Shin, Boston University graduate student Prashant Vaidyanathan, Boston University associate professor Douglas Densmore, and National Institute of Standards and Technology researchers Vanya Paralanov, Elizabeth Strychalski, and David Ross.

Press Release:


Imagine manipulating a bacterium to function like a camera, or to engulf and destroy tumours with high specificity. Similar to installing an app on a cell phone to give it new capabilities, cutting edge cell programming technology can now give living cells new functions—whatever function scientists desire. Carte Blanche meets the biological engineers creating a programming language that allows living cells to be reprogrammed and who’ve made their technology available to all online.


Script:


V/O:
These are images of Albert Einstein captured on ordinary photographic film…. including this iconic 1951 photograph….

But this image of Einstein was recorded in an unprecedented way. By a colony of live e-coli bacteria in a Petri dish.

And these images were also recorded by living bacteria.
Link:
It sounds like science fiction, doesn’t it? But it is not. It is entirely possible to alter e-coli bacteria genetically to become a sort of a bacterial camera.
V/O:
At the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Boston in the USA, Prof Christopher Voigt is a biological engineer specializing in synthetic biology. He created this living camera.
Voigt:
This just involves putting a light sensor into a strain of bacteria that comes from the human gut and we connected that light sensor into the control of an enzyme that turns the pigment black. And so when you shine the image onto a plate of growing bacteria, it recorded that image.
V/O:
He programmed bacteria to become light sensitive and to react like photographic film.

Christopher and his team are not really interested in photography, but they built their bacterial camera to see if they could programme live cells to have complex additional functionalities.

And, their technology has far more important applications – like programming bacteria to sniff out cancer cells and kill them.

They can also programme plants to release insecticides when attacked and control human cells to manufacture medicine for self-healing when needed.
LINK:
A good analogy of what they did is this... a phone. It has certain basic functionalities, but you can install an app that gives it additional functions. You can add a flashlight.
V/O:
And this is what Christopher basically did with the bacteria. He installed a biological “app” in each of them that manipulated their DNA to add to their functions.

Prof Resia Pretorius who heads the Centre for Applied Morphology Research at the University of Pretoria says it is possible to manipulate the DNA of living cells.
Resia:
We can change the DNA sequence and we can change the expression therefore of proteins.
V/O:
And these changes to proteins in turn alter the characteristics and behaviour of cells. But it is a very difficult and slow process.
Resia
In the past it would have taken years to create just a single difference in the DNA sequence, and to determine exactly what the function would be.
V/O:
But this year Christopher and his team announced that they had managed to find a way to introduce really complex changes in the DNA of cells and do this faster than ever before. And the basis of this they found in the nature of DNA itself.
Christopher:
What we found over time is that biology was not this mysterious black box that functioned under no principles. In a biological system you have bio-molecular actions and you have proteins and DNA and RNA and they are all binding to each other in a certain pattern.
LINK:
For Christopher this was a major breakthrough because this opened the way for him to combine other big interest – computers -- with biological systems.
V/O:
Computers run on a variety of circuits that regulate the flow of electrons in certain patterns.
Voigt:
So a circuit implements a computational operation and it is circuits that allow your computer to do the computing that you see in order to write the programmes that you run
V/O:
And in cells the biomolecular interactions also follow very specific patterns.
Voigt:
And it is through that pattern you can get the same computational configurations that you could get with an electronic system.
LINK:
Based on this Christopher and his team surmised that it should also be possible to create programmes that you can introduce into biological systems or cells.
V/O:
These programmes would programme them in the same way you programme computers or cell phones or robots.

They experimented and this year they succeeded in developing a programming language for cells.
Voigt
We can programme cells as though they are robots in order to perform specific functions.
V/O:
Like programming e-coli bacteria to act like camera film.

And they have developed a software package to automate the process.
Voigt:
The way the software works is that you can go online. You first have to select what sensors you want to be the inputs. So, say I want cells to respond to Oxygen and light. You have to put those sensors in.

And then you write the circuit that you want using the Verilog language and you select the organism that you are working with.
V/O:
When you hit RUN the computer works out what needs to be done and after about a minute produces the code for a DNA sequence.
LINK:
This is what it looks like – this string of letters represents part of a DNA sequence that codes for all the additional functions you want a cell to perform.
LINK
In the past it would have taken years to create this kind of sequence but now with the push of a button a software programme can create it for you.
Voigt:
So then what you have to do is take that DNA sequence and you email it to your favourite DNA synthesis company.
V/O:
A synthesis company is able to create synthetic DNA sequences based on the code you send to them.
Voigt:
Anywhere from two to seven days later you will get a tube back in the mail and it looks like it has nothing in it but at the bottom there is a tiny amount of DNA that, when you add water, it mixes in with the water.
LINK:
You will now have something like this – a tube with millions of DNA sequences that will enable cells to have new functions. This DNA “app” that can now be installed in live cells.
V/O:
And it is fairly simple to introduce the DNA into the cells.
Voigt:
You then take that drop of DNA and water, mix it with cells, zap the cells with electricity. They form pores, the DNA is sucked into the cells and that’s it. Now the cells are going to run that program.
V/O
When one does research in the lab with cells, it is called in vitro research.

When using live animals for research it is called in vivo research.

But what Christopher is doing is called in silico research.
Resia:
In silico is designing new compounds and molecules on the computer. So the research done by Christopher at MIT is an example of a type of in silico experiment and it is ground-breaking research new research.
V/O:
Because a computer now creates the code for DNA sequences, it can design combinations of functionalities that were not possible before.
Resia:
The possibilities are really…. anything is possible.
V/O:
In medicine it is possible to programme bacteria to sense the presence of a tumour. Its presence could be signalled by a series of environmental conditions such as a lack of oxygen, temperature and certain chemicals. They can respond to this complex situation.
Voigt:
So they don’t want to respond to any one of those, they want to respond to all of them.
V/O:
For example the programmed bacteria will produce a toxin or therapeutic agent to destroy cancer cells only where there is a lack of oxygen and where the other conditions are also present.
Voigt:
So, what our software would allow them to do is to take all of those signals and build the circuit that is going to respond when each one is in the proper state and then produce a therapeutic in response.
V/O:
And this has enormous potential for agriculture as well. For example, one can coat seeds with specially programmed bacteria. Should the crops come under attack from insects the bacteria can sense that.
Resia:
It could perhaps then activate a chemical toxic reaction that the insects would not be able to eat the crops.
LINK:
Christopher’s software for programming living e-coli to do all kinds of things is available online for free and they encourage experimentation with it.
Voigt:
Oh, absolutely! Schools and universities in South Africa would be free to use it. We see it as a huge potential learning tool to allow people to try things that would normally have taken a very long time, they now can do in a matter of weeks.

That’s what’s really different about this,” Voigt says. “You could be a student in high school and go onto the Web-based server and type out the program you want, and it spits back the DNA sequence.” The language is based on Verilog, which is commonly used to program computer chips. To create a version of the language that would work for cells, the researchers designed computing elements such as logic gates and sensors that can be encoded in a bacterial cell’s DNA. The sensors can detect different compounds, such as oxygen or glucose, as well as light, temperature, acidity, and other environmental conditions. Users can also add their own sensors. “It’s very customizable,” Voigt says. The biggest challenge, he says, was designing the 14 logic gates used in the circuits so that they wouldn’t interfere with each other once placed in the complex environment of a living cell. In the current version of the programming language, these genetic parts are optimized for E. coli, but the researchers are working on expanding the language for other strains of bacteria, including Bacteroides, commonly found in the human gut, and Pseudomonas, which often lives in plant roots, as well as the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. This would allow users to write a single program and then compile it for different organisms to get the right DNA sequence for each one. Biological circuits Using this language, the researchers programmed 60 circuits with different functions, and 45 of them worked correctly the first time they were tested. Many of the circuits were designed to measure one or more environmental conditions, such as oxygen level or glucose concentration, and respond accordingly. Another circuit was designed to rank three different inputs and then respond based on the priority of each one. One of the new circuits is the largest biological circuit ever built, containing seven logic gates and about 12,000 base pairs of DNA. Another advantage of this technique is its speed. Until now, “it would take years to build these types of circuits. Now you just hit the button and immediately get a DNA sequence to test,” Voigt says. His team plans to work on several different applications using this approach: bacteria that can be swallowed to aid in digestion of lactose; bacteria that can live on plant roots and produce insecticide if they sense the plant is under attack; and yeast that can be engineered to shut off when they are producing too many toxic byproducts in a fermentation reactor. The lead author of the Science paper is MIT graduate student Alec Nielsen. Other authors are former MIT postdoc Bryan Der, MIT postdoc Jonghyeon Shin, Boston University graduate student Prashant Vaidyanathan, Boston University associate professor Douglas Densmore, and National Institute of Standards and Technology researchers Vanya Paralanov, Elizabeth Strychalski, and David Ross.
